title: Pneumoperitoneum on the radiograph
text:
A perforated viscus (peptic ulcer, diverticulum, colonic tumour, ischaemic bowel) releases gas that rises to the highest point of the peritoneal cavity. On an erect chest radiograph, taken after the patient has sat upright for several minutes, a thin crescent of gas appears beneath the diaphragm, most easily seen on the right between the diaphragm and the liver. On the left, the gastric fundus bubble is the normal mimic. Very ill patients can have a left lateral decubitus film, gas then collecting over the liver.
On a supine abdominal film free gas outlines both sides of the bowel wall (Rigler sign), the falciform ligament, or in neonates forms a large central oval lucency (football sign). CT is far more sensitive and shows the site. Colon interposed between the liver and diaphragm (Chilaiditi sign) mimics free gas but haustra are seen crossing it. Free gas is normal for several days after laparotomy or laparoscopy, and about a quarter of perforations show no free gas on plain film.

title: Lobar collapse and the silhouette sign
text:
An interface is only visible on a radiograph where tissues of different density meet. When airless lung lies against the heart or diaphragm, that border disappears (the silhouette sign), localising the lobe: the right middle lobe borders the right heart border, the lingula the left heart border, and the lower lobes the hemidiaphragms and descending aorta.
Collapse patterns: right upper lobe collapses upward and medially, raising the horizontal fissure (with a central mass the fissure forms a reversed S, the Golden S sign); left upper lobe collapses forward, giving a veil-like haze over the left hemithorax, sometimes with a crescent of aerated lower lobe around the aortic knuckle (luftsichel sign); left lower lobe collapses behind the heart as a triangular density with a 'sail' edge and loss of the medial hemidiaphragm; right middle lobe collapse effaces the right heart border. Volume loss pulls the fissures, hilum, trachea and mediastinum toward the collapsed lobe. New lobar collapse in an adult smoker is an obstructing tumour until bronchoscopy proves otherwise; in children and ventilated patients, mucus plugs and foreign bodies are commoner.

title: Consolidation and air bronchograms
text:
In consolidation the alveoli are filled with fluid, pus, blood or cells while the bronchi remain aerated, so branching dark air bronchograms are seen within the white lobe; volume is preserved (no shift), unlike collapse. The pattern respects fissures: right middle lobe consolidation abuts the horizontal fissure above and obliterates the right heart border, and on the lateral view appears as a wedge overlying the heart between the horizontal and oblique fissures.
Lobar pneumonia is classically pneumococcal; upper lobe cavitating consolidation suggests tuberculosis or Klebsiella, and multiple cavities Staphylococcus aureus. Other causes of airspace opacity include pulmonary oedema (perihilar, bilateral), haemorrhage, adenocarcinoma and organising pneumonia. Radiographic resolution lags behind clinical recovery by weeks, so a follow-up radiograph at about six weeks is advised in smokers and older patients to make sure the opacity was not hiding a tumour.

title: Pneumothorax on the radiograph
text:
The diagnostic sign is a thin white visceral pleural line with no lung markings beyond it. Skin folds, the scapular border and bullae are the mimics; a skin fold usually extends beyond the chest wall and has no pleural line. Size is measured at the level of the hilum: an interpleural distance of 2 cm or more is a large pneumothorax in current UK guidance. Small pneumothoraces are easier to see on an expiratory film or CT.
On a supine film (trauma, intensive care), air collects anteriorly and inferiorly, producing an abnormally deep, lucent costophrenic angle (deep sulcus sign) and a sharply outlined heart border and hemidiaphragm; many are missed on supine films, and ultrasound (absent lung sliding) is more sensitive.
Tension pneumothorax is a CLINICAL diagnosis (hypotension, hypoxia, deviated trachea, absent breath sounds) and needs immediate decompression without waiting for imaging; if a film is taken, the mediastinum is pushed to the opposite side and the hemidiaphragm is flattened or inverted.

title: Mediastinal shift: pushed or pulled?
text:
The trachea and mediastinum move toward the side of volume LOSS and away from the side of a space-occupying process. Shift to the left therefore means either something on the right is pushing (tension pneumothorax, massive pleural effusion, large diaphragmatic hernia or mass) or something on the left is pulling (collapse of the left lung or lobe, pneumonectomy, lung hypoplasia or fibrosis).
The opacity of the affected hemithorax separates them: a white-out with shift AWAY from it is a large effusion or mass; a white-out with shift TOWARD it is collapse (obstructed main bronchus) or pneumonectomy; a white-out without shift suggests consolidation with collapse, effusion plus collapse balancing each other, or mesothelioma encasing the lung. A black hemithorax with shift away is tension pneumothorax. The trachea at the thoracic inlet and the position of the heart relative to the spine are checked on every chest radiograph, remembering that patient rotation (unequal distances between the medial clavicle ends and the spinous processes) can mimic shift.

title: Pleural effusion on imaging and pleural aspiration
text:
On an erect posteroanterior film about 200 mL of fluid is needed to blunt the costophrenic angle (about 50 mL on the lateral view, where the posterior angle is deepest). Larger effusions form a homogeneous opacity with a meniscus curving up the lateral chest wall; massive effusions push the mediastinum away. On a supine film the fluid layers posteriorly as a hazy veil over the whole hemithorax with visible vessels. A subpulmonic effusion mimics a raised hemidiaphragm with its peak displaced laterally. Ultrasound detects small volumes, shows septations and guides aspiration.
Small bilateral effusions with cardiomegaly suggest heart failure (transudate); a large unilateral effusion suggests malignancy, infection (parapneumonic effusion or empyema) or tuberculosis. Aspirated fluid is compared with serum using Light's criteria (exudate if fluid-to-serum protein ratio above 0.5 or LDH ratio above 0.6, or fluid LDH above two-thirds of the upper normal serum limit); pH below 7.2 in a parapneumonic effusion indicates the need for drainage. Aspiration is done above a rib in the posterior chest wall below the fluid level, under ultrasound guidance.

title: Bowel obstruction on the plain film
text:
Small bowel loops lie centrally, have valvulae conniventes (mucosal folds that cross the whole width of the lumen) and are abnormal above about 3 cm in diameter. Large bowel lies peripherally, has haustra (folds that cross only part of the lumen, between the taeniae coli) and is abnormal above about 6 cm, or 9 cm for the caecum (the '3-6-9 rule'); a caecum above about 12 cm is at risk of perforation.
Small bowel obstruction is most often caused by adhesions and hernias (examine the groins); large bowel obstruction by carcinoma, volvulus and diverticular strictures. With a competent ileocaecal valve a colonic obstruction becomes a closed loop and the caecum can burst. A sigmoid volvulus forms a huge inverted U ('coffee bean') arising from the pelvis; caecal volvulus lies centrally or in the left upper quadrant. Pseudo-obstruction (Ogilvie syndrome) dilates the colon without a mechanical block in frail post-operative patients.
CT with contrast is the standard: it identifies the transition point, the cause and signs of strangulation (reduced wall enhancement, mesenteric fluid, pneumatosis), which demand surgery.

title: Abdominal incisions and incisional hernia
text:
Midline laparotomy through the relatively avascular linea alba is quick, extendable and gives access to the whole abdomen, but carries the highest risk of incisional hernia. Muscle-splitting incisions follow the fibres of each layer: the gridiron or Lanz incision over McBurney's point splits external oblique, internal oblique and transversus in turn, preserving their nerves. The Pfannenstiel incision (caesarean section, pelvic surgery) is a low transverse skin and anterior rectus sheath incision with the recti separated in the midline; the iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal nerves can be trapped at its lateral ends. The Kocher (right subcostal) incision for open biliary surgery divides rectus and may denervate part of it if the lower intercostal nerves are cut. Transverse incisions follow Langer lines and the dermatomes, heal with less tension and cause less post-operative pain.
Incisional hernias follow about 10 to 20% of midline laparotomies: risk factors include wound infection, obesity, smoking, steroids, diabetes and emergency surgery; closure with a small-bite technique and a suture-to-wound-length ratio of at least 4:1 reduces them. Laparoscopic port sites of 10 mm or more are closed at the fascia to prevent port-site hernias.

title: Carotid endarterectomy: indications and nerves at risk
text:
Endarterectomy removes atheroma from the carotid bifurcation and proximal internal carotid artery. It clearly benefits patients with a recent TIA or non-disabling stroke in the carotid territory and a stenosis of 50 to 99% (greatest for 70 to 99%), and it should be done within two weeks of symptoms when the risk of recurrence is highest. The benefit in asymptomatic stenosis is small.
The incision runs along the anterior border of sternocleidomastoid. The common facial vein crossing the carotid sheath marks the level of the bifurcation and is divided. Nerves at risk: the hypoglossal nerve crossing both carotid arteries just above the bifurcation (tongue deviates to the operated side), the vagus in the sheath behind the vessels and its recurrent and superior laryngeal branches (hoarseness, weak voice), the marginal mandibular branch of the facial nerve if retraction is high (drooping lower lip), the great auricular nerve (numb ear lobe) and the ansa cervicalis. Other complications are peri-operative stroke, neck haematoma compressing the airway, and cerebral hyperperfusion syndrome (headache, seizures, haemorrhage).

title: Knee aspiration and lipohaemarthrosis
text:
The suprapatellar bursa communicates with the knee joint and extends a hand's breadth above the patella deep to quadriceps, so effusions first fill it and then displace the patella (patellar tap) or cause a bulge on stroking fluid across the joint. Aspiration is performed through a superolateral approach, just under the lateral border of the upper patella into the suprapatellar pouch, with the knee extended and quadriceps relaxed, under strict asepsis because septic arthritis must not be introduced.
Fluid is sent for Gram stain, culture and crystal microscopy. Frank blood suggests an ACL tear, peripheral meniscal tear, fracture or bleeding disorder; fat globules floating on blood indicate marrow fat released by an intra-articular fracture. On a horizontal-beam lateral radiograph taken with the patient supine, a lipohaemarthrosis shows as a straight fat-fluid level in the suprapatellar pouch, a sign of an occult tibial plateau or femoral condyle fracture that should prompt CT.

title: Subacromial bursa: injection, bursitis and cuff tears
text:
The subacromial and subdeltoid bursae usually form one continuous space between the rotator cuff (below) and the acromion, coracoacromial ligament and deltoid (above), allowing the cuff to glide during abduction. Inflamed in subacromial impingement, the bursa causes a painful arc of abduction between about 60 and 120 degrees.
Steroid injection into the bursa is given from a posterior approach, under the posterolateral corner of the acromion aiming toward the coracoid, or under ultrasound guidance; repeated injections weaken the cuff tendons. Normally the bursa does not communicate with the glenohumeral joint; contrast or fluid passing from the joint into the bursa on arthrography or MR arthrography indicates a full-thickness rotator cuff tear. Calcific tendinitis of supraspinatus can rupture into the bursa, causing excruciating acute pain, and ultrasound-guided barbotage can wash it out.

title: Elbow radiograph: fat pads and alignment lines
text:
Fat pads lie outside the synovium in the coronoid and olecranon fossae. On a true lateral film with the elbow at 90 degrees a thin anterior fat pad is normal, but an elevated anterior pad ('sail sign') or any visible posterior fat pad means a joint effusion. After trauma this indicates an intra-articular fracture even when none is seen: usually a radial head or neck fracture in adults and a supracondylar fracture in children.
Two lines check alignment. The anterior humeral line, drawn along the front of the humeral shaft, should pass through the middle third of the capitellum; if it passes through the anterior third or misses it, the capitellum has displaced backward (extension-type supracondylar fracture). The radiocapitellar line, along the axis of the radial neck, should pass through the capitellum in every view; if not, the radial head is dislocated, and the ulna must be checked for a Monteggia fracture. In children, the order in which ossification centres appear (CRITOE: capitellum, radial head, internal (medial) epicondyle, trochlea, olecranon, external epicondyle) helps identify an avulsed medial epicondyle trapped in the joint.

title: Hip radiograph: Shenton line and occult fractures
text:
Shenton line, the smooth arc formed by the inferior border of the superior pubic ramus and the medial border of the femoral neck, is broken in displaced femoral neck fractures and in hip dislocation or dysplasia. Other things to check: the trabecular pattern and cortex of the neck, the lesser trochanter (it becomes more prominent as the leg externally rotates), and the pubic rami, which are a common alternative fracture in the elderly.
Intracapsular fractures are graded by the Garden classification (I incomplete or impacted in valgus, II complete undisplaced, III partly displaced, IV fully displaced); displaced fractures threaten the retinacular blood supply and are generally replaced (hemiarthroplasty or total hip replacement), while undisplaced ones may be fixed. If the radiograph is normal but the patient cannot bear weight, MRI (or CT if MRI is unavailable) should be performed the same day, because occult fractures that displace later have a much worse outcome.

title: Cervical spine imaging after trauma
text:
Clinical decision rules (NEXUS, Canadian C-spine rule) identify patients who need no imaging: alert, not intoxicated, without midline tenderness, focal neurology or a distracting injury, with a low-risk mechanism, and able to rotate the neck 45 degrees each way. In adults who need imaging, CT is now the first test; MRI is added for neurological deficits or suspected ligamentous injury.
When radiographs are used (for example in children), an adequate lateral film must show the whole of C7 and the top of T1, which the shoulders often hide (a swimmer's view or traction on the arms helps). Four smooth curves are traced: the anterior vertebral line, the posterior vertebral line (front of the canal), the spinolaminar line (back of the canal) and the tips of the spinous processes. A step, widening of the interspinous space, a prevertebral soft tissue thickness greater than about 7 mm at C2 or 22 mm at C6, or a widened atlantodental interval suggest injury. The open-mouth odontoid view shows the dens and the lateral masses of C1 (their overhang implies a Jefferson fracture). Children have normal pseudosubluxation of C2 on C3.
